title: This Computer Runs on DNA and Fits in a Drop of Water
summary: What if you could do math without a calculator, a phone, or even electricity? Scientists have built a computer that uses DNA — the same stuff that carries your genes — to solve problems. And it all happens in a tiny drop of water. The computer is called the Scaffolded DNA Computer, or SDC. It's made of short DNA strands that mix with a longer DNA strand in salt water. When the water is heated and cooled, the strands compete to connect in the right way. The final shape gives the answer. "The DNA molecules compete with each other to select a winner," said Damien Woods, a professor at Maynooth University in Ireland. The SDC can do simple math, like 10 + 3, in about 30 seconds. That's slow compared to a regular computer, which does it in a flash. But the DNA computer uses way less energy. It doesn't need constant power to keep going. Instead, it uses the laws of physics to settle into the correct answer. The team tested over 700 calculations, including addition, multiplication, and division. A really hard problem took up to 14 hours. Scientists think DNA computers could one day store data or even work inside living cells. "They're not trying to replace electronic ones," said Abeer Eshra, a co-author. "But they could be used in biological environments." So next time you do math, think about the tiny DNA computer that does it with just a drop of water!
why_it_matters: Computers today use lots of electricity, so if DNA computers work, they could help store information in a totally new way and even run tiny medical devices inside our bodies.

background_read: DNA is the long, twisty molecule inside every living thing, storing the instructions for building and running a body.
Maynooth University (a university in Ireland) is where the team that built this DNA computer works; scientists in several countries have been trying to compute with DNA for many years.
Regular computers use electricity and get hot, while nature packs enormous amounts of information into DNA — all the instructions for a tree or a person fit inside cells too small to see.
Article_Structure: WHO: A team led by professor Damien Woods at Maynooth University in Ireland, with co-author Abeer Eshra.
WHAT: They built the Scaffolded DNA Computer (SDC), which uses DNA strands in salt water to solve math problems.
WHERE: In a tiny drop of water — no electricity or normal computer parts needed.
WHY: It uses far less energy than a regular computer and might one day store data or work inside living cells.

perspectives.description: They are excited that mixing DNA strands can produce correct answers by itself, like a tiny chemistry puzzle solving itself.
They point out that 30 seconds for 10 + 3 is much slower than a normal computer, so DNA computers won't replace the laptop at home.
They see the real promise in biology — a computer that works in water and living cells could help inside the human body one day.
